title: RAG: Introduction
description: Giving a model access to documents it was never trained on, and why that solves a real problem.

lessons.title: What RAG is, and why it exists
lessons.description: Find the material, put it in the prompt -- and why that is the safe category.
lessons.content:
## Learn

**RAG** stands for retrieval-augmented generation. It means: before asking the model, find the relevant material and put it in the prompt.

That is the whole idea. The rest of this module is how to do it well.

### The problem it solves

A model knows what was in its training data, up to its cutoff. It does not know:

- Your company's documents
- Your lecture notes
- Anything written after its cutoff
- Anything private, internal or specific to you

Three ways to fix that, from module 2:

**Fine-tuning.** Train the model further on your material. Expensive, needs expertise, and has to be redone when the material changes.

**Put everything in the prompt.** Works for a few pages. Fails for a few hundred, on cost and context limits.

**Retrieval.** Find the few relevant passages and put only those in the prompt. Cheap, updates instantly, works at any scale.

Retrieval wins for almost every case, which is why RAG is everywhere.

### What it looks like

Without RAG:

> **You:** What is our refund policy for damaged goods?
> **Model:** *(invents something plausible)*

With RAG:

> **You:** What is our refund policy for damaged goods?
> **System:** searches your documents, finds three relevant passages
> **Model receives:** those passages, plus the question
> **Model:** answers from the passages, citing them

The model did not learn anything. It was handed the answer and asked to read it.

### Why this is the most important technique in the course

Three reasons.

**It converts recall into transformation.** Module 3's central distinction. The model is no longer remembering -- it is reading material in front of it. That is the safe category, and the hallucination rate falls sharply.

**It gives you citations.** You know which passage an answer came from, so you can check it. Without that you are trusting.

**It updates instantly.** Change the document, the next answer changes. No retraining.

### What it does not fix

**A wrong document gives a wrong answer**, now with a citation making it more credible. Grounding is not fact-checking.

**Retrieval can miss.** If the right passage is not found, the model answers without it -- and will often answer anyway.

**It can still misread** what it retrieved.

**It cannot synthesise across a whole corpus.** "What is the overall theme of these 500 documents" is not a retrieval question, because there is no small set of passages that answers it.

### You have already used one

NotebookLM, from module 5, is RAG with a polished interface. Upload sources, ask questions, get answers grounded in them with citations, and get told when the sources do not cover something.

That "told when it does not know" behaviour is not a smarter model. It is the constraint.

## Demonstrate

See the difference directly. Ten minutes.

Find a document the model could not know: an internal policy, your own notes, a recent paper, a club's rules.

**Without RAG:** in a fresh conversation, ask a specific question about it without providing it. Note what you get -- usually a confident, plausible, invented answer.

**With RAG, by hand:** in a fresh conversation, paste the relevant section and ask the same question.

The second is right. The first was fiction delivered in the same tone.

You just performed retrieval manually. The rest of this module automates finding the right section when there are five hundred documents.

## Practice

List five questions you would want answered from material a model cannot know -- your notes, your workplace's documents, a set of papers.

For each, write:

1. Which document holds the answer
2. Roughly how much of it is relevant -- a paragraph, a page, a section
3. Whether a keyword search would find it, or whether it needs meaning

Question 3 is the interesting one. Where the answer uses different words from your question, keyword search fails and embeddings from module 2 are what make retrieval work.

## What to remember

- RAG: find the relevant material and put it in the prompt before asking
- It converts recall into transformation, which is the safe category
- It gives citations you can check, and updates the moment the document changes
- A wrong source gives a confidently wrong answer with a citation attached
- If retrieval misses, the model will often answer anyway

lessons.title: The RAG pipeline
lessons.description: Five stages, their characteristic failures, and a complete system in thirty lines.
lessons.content:
## Learn

The pipeline has five stages. Everything in RAG is one of these.

```
Documents -> Chunks -> Embeddings -> Vector database -> LLM
```

### 1. Documents

Whatever you have: PDFs, web pages, notes, transcripts, spreadsheets.

The work here is extraction and cleaning. A PDF with two columns extracts into interleaved nonsense unless handled. Headers and footers repeat on every page and pollute retrieval.

**Bad extraction is the most common cause of a bad RAG system**, and it is invisible later: everything downstream looks fine, and the answers are wrong.

### 2. Chunks

Split each document into pieces, because you retrieve chunks, not documents.

Size is a genuine trade-off:

**Too small** and a chunk lacks the context to be understood. "It must be returned within 14 days" -- what must?

**Too large** and it contains mostly irrelevant text, which dilutes the embedding and wastes context.

A reasonable starting point is a few hundred words with some overlap. Lesson 5 covers this properly.

**Chunk at natural boundaries** where you can: paragraphs, sections, headings. A chunk cut mid-sentence retrieves badly.

### 3. Embeddings

Each chunk becomes a list of numbers capturing its meaning, exactly as module 2 described.

Done once, when you add the document. The query gets embedded at question time.

Two rules:

**Use the same model for chunks and queries.** Embeddings from different models are not comparable. This is a real and confusing bug.

**Changing the model means re-embedding everything.**

### 4. Vector database

Stores the embeddings and finds the closest ones to a query, fast.

You could do this with a loop over a list -- and for a few thousand chunks, you should. Lesson 4 covers when you actually need a database.

### 5. The LLM

Retrieved chunks go into the prompt with the question, and the model answers from them.

The prompt matters as much as the retrieval. Lesson 5 covers it.

### The full flow, at question time

```
1. User asks a question
2. Embed the question
3. Find the N most similar chunks
4. Put those chunks and the question in a prompt
5. Model answers from the chunks
6. Return the answer with the sources
```

Steps 2 and 3 take milliseconds. Step 5 is where the time goes.

### Where it goes wrong

Each stage has a characteristic failure, and knowing which is which saves hours:

**Extraction:** garbled text, so nothing retrieves properly.

**Chunking:** answers split across two chunks, so neither contains the whole answer.

**Embedding:** mismatched models, so similarity is meaningless.

**Retrieval:** the right chunk exists and is not in the top N.

**Generation:** the right chunk was retrieved and the model ignored or misread it.

**Diagnose in that order.** People start at the end and blame the model. The fault is usually at the start.

## Demonstrate

Build the whole pipeline in about thirty lines, with no database and no framework. This is a complete, working RAG system.

```python
# pip install sentence-transformers
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

# 1-2. Documents, already chunked by paragraph.
chunks = [
    "Refunds are available within 30 days of purchase for unused items.",
    "Damaged goods may be returned at any time for a full refund or replacement.",
    "Our offices are open Monday to Friday, 9am to 5pm.",
    "Shipping is free on orders over 50 pounds. Standard delivery takes 3-5 days.",
]

# 3. Embed the chunks, once.
chunk_vectors = model.encode(chunks)


def retrieve(question: str, top_k: int = 2) -> list[tuple[str, float]]:
    """Find the chunks most similar in meaning to the question."""
    question_vector = model.encode(question)
    scores = util.cos_sim(question_vector, chunk_vectors)[0]
    ranked = sorted(zip(chunks, scores), key=lambda pair: pair[1], reverse=True)
    return [(chunk, float(score)) for chunk, score in ranked[:top_k]]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for chunk, score in retrieve("What if my order arrives broken?"):
        print(f"{score:.3f}  {chunk}")
```

Expected output, approximately:

```
0.498  Damaged goods may be returned at any time for a full refund or replacement.
0.231  Refunds are available within 30 days of purchase for unused items.
```

Look at the top result. The question said "arrives broken". The chunk says "damaged goods". **No shared words.** Keyword search finds nothing; embeddings find it immediately.

That is the whole reason this works.

## Practice

Run the code above with your own chunks -- ten paragraphs from something you actually have.

Write five questions and check the retrieval for each.

Then deliberately find a failure: a question whose answer is in your chunks but which retrieves the wrong one.

:::hint I cannot make it fail
Try negation -- "what is *not* covered" against a chunk listing what is covered. Or try a question whose answer spans two chunks. Or use a question containing a word that appears prominently in an irrelevant chunk. Embeddings are notoriously weak on negation, and finding that yourself is worth more than being told.
:::

## What to remember

- Five stages: documents, chunks, embeddings, vector store, LLM
- Bad extraction is the most common cause of a bad RAG system and is invisible later
- You retrieve chunks, not documents, so chunk size is a real trade-off
- Use the same embedding model for chunks and queries, always
- Diagnose failures from the start of the pipeline, not the end

lessons.title: RAG versus plain prompting
lessons.description: When pasting is better, and the hybrid that often beats both.
lessons.content:
## Learn

When do you need RAG, and when is pasting the text into the prompt enough?

### Just paste it

If your material fits comfortably in the context window and does not change often, paste it. No pipeline, no embeddings, no database.

**Use this when:**

- The material is a few pages
- It is the same material every time
- You are exploring rather than building
- You want the model to consider **all** of it, not a selection

That last point matters and is often missed. Pasting means the model sees everything. Retrieval means it sees a selection, and if the selection is wrong the answer is wrong.

### Use RAG

**Use this when:**

- The material is too large for the context window
- There is a lot of it and only a little is relevant to any question
- It changes and you do not want to re-paste
- Many people ask different questions of the same corpus
- You need to know which source an answer came from
- Sending everything every time would be too expensive

### The cost argument

Worth making concrete, because it decides many real cases.

Suppose you have 200 pages of documentation and a hundred questions a day.

**Pasting everything:** every question sends 200 pages. A hundred times a day. You pay for all of it, every time, and most of it is irrelevant to each question.

**RAG:** every question sends three paragraphs. Roughly a hundredth of the tokens.

At small volumes this does not matter. At any real volume it decides the question.

### The hybrid, which is often best

Not either/or.

**Retrieve, then include generously.** Rather than three tiny chunks, retrieve the five most relevant sections and include them in full. Uses more context, much more likely to contain the answer.

**Retrieve a document, then paste the whole document.** If your unit is a policy document of two pages, retrieve *which* document, then include all of it. Best of both: you found the right thing and the model sees all of it.

This second pattern is underrated and often the right answer for a modest corpus of medium-sized documents.

### The decision

```
Does it fit in context comfortably?
  Yes -> Does it change often?
           No  -> Paste it
           Yes -> Paste it, and automate the pasting
  No  -> Is it many small documents, or a few large ones?
           Many small -> RAG over chunks
           Few large  -> RAG to pick the document, then paste it whole
```

### The mistake to avoid

**Building RAG when pasting would do.**

RAG has real costs: an extraction pipeline, chunking decisions, an embedding model, a store, and a new failure mode where retrieval misses and you never find out.

If your material is thirty pages and it fits, paste it. You will have a better system with a tenth of the work.

This is exactly module 11's lesson about agents and workflows, in a different costume: **use the simplest thing that works.**

## Demonstrate

Compare the two on the same material.

Take a document of roughly ten pages.

**Version A:** paste the whole thing and ask five questions, in five fresh conversations.

**Version B:** chunk it by paragraph using lesson 2's code, retrieve the top three for each question, and paste only those with the question.

Score both against what you know the answers to be.

For ten pages, A will usually be at least as good and possibly better, because it sees everything. That result is the lesson: **at this size, RAG is not helping you.**

Now imagine the same comparison at a thousand pages, where A is not possible at all.

## Practice

Take three collections of material you actually have -- your notes for a course, a set of documents at work, a folder of papers.

For each, answer:

1. Roughly how many words? Divide by 0.75 for a rough token estimate.
2. Does that fit in a typical context window?
3. How often does it change?
4. How many questions a day would be asked of it?
5. Do you need to know the source of an answer?

Then decide: paste, RAG, or hybrid. Write one sentence justifying each.

Most people find at least one where they assumed they needed RAG and do not.

## What to remember

- If it fits in context and you want everything considered, paste it
- RAG earns its place on size, change rate, volume, and the need for citations
- Cost at volume decides many real cases: a hundredth of the tokens per question
- The hybrid -- retrieve the document, then include it whole -- is often the best answer
- Building RAG when pasting would do is the common and expensive mistake

lessons.title: Vector databases
lessons.description: When a list and a loop is the right answer, and when it is not.
lessons.content:
## Learn

A vector database stores embeddings and finds the nearest ones to a query, quickly.

### What "nearest" means

From module 2: similar meanings produce vectors that are close together. Given a query vector, the database finds the stored vectors closest to it.

The naive way is to compare against every stored vector. That is exact and gets slow as the collection grows.

Vector databases use **approximate nearest neighbour** search: much faster, occasionally missing a result it should have found. For almost every use, the trade is worth it.

### When you actually need one

**Under about ten thousand chunks: you do not.**

A list of vectors and a loop is exact, simple, has no extra dependency, and is fast enough. This is what lesson 2's code does.

**You need one when:**

- You have hundreds of thousands of chunks
- You need sub-second search at that scale
- You need filtering: "only documents from this department, after this date"
- Several applications share the same store
- Embeddings must survive a restart without re-computing

That last one is the most common real trigger. Re-embedding a large corpus every time your application starts is slow and expensive.

### The kinds

**In-memory libraries.** FAISS and similar. A library, not a server. Fast, simple, and you handle persistence.

**Embedded databases.** Chroma, LanceDB and similar. Run inside your application, save to disk, no server. The right choice for most projects that have outgrown a list.

**Hosted services.** Pinecone, Weaviate and others. A managed service. For scale and teams.

**Extensions to databases you already have.** PostgreSQL with `pgvector`, and similar for others. Often the best answer for an organisation: no new system, and your vectors sit next to your other data.

That last option is under-considered and frequently correct.

### Metadata

Whatever you use, store more than the vector:

```python
{
    "text": "the chunk itself",
    "source": "handbook.pdf",
    "page": 14,
    "section": "Refunds",
    "updated": "2026-03-01",
}
```

**Source and location are essential** -- without them you cannot cite, and citation is half the value of RAG.

**Dates matter** because stale documents are a real failure mode.

**Filterable fields** let you narrow before searching, which improves both speed and relevance.

### The decision

Start with a list. Move to an embedded database when you need persistence or scale. Move to hosted when you need more than one application or more than one machine.

The same progression as everything else in this course: simplest thing that works.

## Demonstrate

Persistence without a database, which covers most projects.

```python
import json
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util

MODEL_NAME = "all-MiniLM-L6-v2"
STORE = Path("store.npz")
META = Path("store.json")


def build(chunks: list[dict]) -> None:
    """Embed chunks and save vectors and metadata to disk.

    Each chunk is a dict with at least 'text', plus any metadata.
    """
    model = SentenceTransformer(MODEL_NAME)
    vectors = model.encode([chunk["text"] for chunk in chunks])

    np.savez_compressed(STORE, vectors=vectors)
    # The model name is saved with the metadata so a later search can
    # refuse to compare vectors built by a different model.
    META.write_text(
        json.dumps({"model": MODEL_NAME, "chunks": chunks}, ensure_ascii=False),
        encoding="utf-8",
    )


def search(question: str, top_k: int = 3) -> list[dict]:
    """Return the top_k chunks, each with its score and metadata."""
    if not STORE.exists() or not META.exists():
        raise FileNotFoundError("No store found. Run build() first.")

    meta = json.loads(META.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    if meta["model"] != MODEL_NAME:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"Store was built with {meta['model']!r} but this code uses "
            f"{MODEL_NAME!r}. Rebuild the store."
        )

    vectors = np.load(STORE)["vectors"]
    model = SentenceTransformer(MODEL_NAME)
    scores = util.cos_sim(model.encode(question), vectors)[0]

    ranked = sorted(
        ({**chunk, "score": float(score)} for chunk, score in zip(meta["chunks"], scores)),
        key=lambda item: item["score"],
        reverse=True,
    )
    return ranked[:top_k]
```

The model-name check is the important part. Comparing vectors from two different embedding models produces plausible scores that are meaningless -- a bug that is extremely confusing to diagnose, because nothing fails, the results are simply wrong.

## Practice

### Exercise: retrieval with a relevance floor

Retrieval always returns something, even when nothing relevant exists. Add a threshold.

```python
def search_with_floor(question: str, chunks: list[dict], vectors,
                      top_k: int = 3, min_score: float = 0.25) -> dict:
    """Search, discarding results below min_score.

    Returns {'results': [...], 'confident': bool}. 'confident' is False
    when nothing cleared the floor, so the caller can say it does not
    know rather than answering from irrelevant material.
    """
    # Your code here
    ...
```

Expected output when nothing is relevant:

```
{'results': [], 'confident': False}
```

:::hint Getting started
Score everything as before, then filter with `score >= min_score` before slicing to `top_k`. `confident` is simply whether the filtered list is non-empty. The order matters: filter first, then take the top k, or you may discard good results to make room for bad ones.
:::

:::solution
```python
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util

_model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")


def search_with_floor(question: str, chunks: list[dict], vectors,
                      top_k: int = 3, min_score: float = 0.25) -> dict:
    """Search, discarding results below min_score."""
    if not chunks:
        return {"results": [], "confident": False}

    scores = util.cos_sim(_model.encode(question), vectors)[0]

    scored = [
        {**chunk, "score": float(score)}
        for chunk, score in zip(chunks, scores)
        if float(score) >= min_score
    ]
    scored.sort(key=lambda item: item["score"], reverse=True)
    results = scored[:top_k]

    return {"results": results, "confident": bool(results)}
```

Filtering before sorting and slicing is the detail that matters. Taking the top three and *then* filtering can return one weak result where filtering first would have returned three good ones from further down the list.

The floor value is not universal -- it depends on the embedding model and your material. Calibrate it by running questions you know have no answer in your corpus and seeing what scores they produce.
:::

### Debugging exercise

This is meant to add new chunks to an existing store. It has **two** bugs.

```python
def add_chunks(new_chunks, store_path, meta_path):
    model = SentenceTransformer(MODEL_NAME)
    new_vectors = model.encode([c["text"] for c in new_chunks])
    np.savez_compressed(store_path, vectors=new_vectors)
    meta = json.loads(meta_path.read_text())
    meta["chunks"] = new_chunks
    meta_path.write_text(json.dumps(meta))
```

:::hint What to look at
Call it twice with different chunks and then search. What is in the store afterwards?
:::

:::solution
**Bug one: it overwrites the vectors instead of appending.** `np.savez_compressed` with only the new vectors discards everything already stored. After one call, your entire existing corpus is gone.

**Bug two: it overwrites the metadata the same way**, so even the record of what was there is lost. The two bugs are the same mistake made twice, which is why adding is a genuinely error-prone operation.

```python
import numpy as np


def add_chunks(new_chunks: list[dict], store_path, meta_path) -> None:
    """Append new chunks to an existing store."""
    model = SentenceTransformer(MODEL_NAME)
    new_vectors = model.encode([chunk["text"] for chunk in new_chunks])

    meta = json.loads(meta_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    if meta["model"] != MODEL_NAME:
        raise RuntimeError("Store was built with a different embedding model.")

    existing = np.load(store_path)["vectors"]
    np.savez_compressed(store_path, vectors=np.vstack([existing, new_vectors]))

    meta["chunks"] = meta["chunks"] + new_chunks
    meta_path.write_text(json.dumps(meta, ensure_ascii=False), encoding="utf-8")
```

Two things worth noting beyond the fix. The vectors and the metadata must stay in the **same order** -- `vstack` appends and the list concatenation appends, so index *i* still refers to the same chunk in both. If they ever drift apart, every citation points at the wrong text, and nothing errors.

And the missing `encoding="utf-8"` in the original is a third, quieter problem: on some platforms it will read and write in a different encoding and corrupt non-English text.
:::

## What to remember

- Under about ten thousand chunks, a list and a loop is the right answer
- You need a database for scale, filtering, sharing, or persistence across restarts
- An extension to a database you already run is often the best organisational answer
- Store source and location as metadata or you cannot cite
- Keep vectors and metadata in the same order, or every citation silently points at the wrong text

lessons.title: Building a document question-answering app
lessons.description: Chunking that retrieves, a prompt that refuses, and two refusal paths.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Putting it together: a working document question-answering application.

### Chunking properly

The decision that most affects quality.

**Split at natural boundaries.** Paragraphs, then sentences if a paragraph is too long. Never mid-sentence if avoidable.

**Overlap.** Include the end of the previous chunk at the start of the next, typically 10 to 20 per cent. This stops an answer that straddles a boundary being lost from both chunks.

**Keep context in the chunk.** A chunk saying "it must be returned within 14 days" is useless alone. Prepend the document title and section heading to each chunk before embedding:

```
[Employee Handbook > Section 4: Equipment]
It must be returned within 14 days of leaving.
```

This single change improves retrieval quality more than almost anything else, and most people do not do it.

**Size:** a few hundred words is a reasonable default. Tune it by testing.

### The prompt

Retrieval gets the material there. The prompt decides what happens next.

```python
RAG_PROMPT = Template("""Answer the question using only the sources below.

Sources:
$sources

Question: $question

Rules:
- Use only the sources above. Do not use other knowledge.
- Cite the source number for each claim, like [1].
- If the sources do not contain the answer, say exactly:
  "The provided sources do not answer this question."
  Do not guess and do not partially answer.
- If the sources disagree, say so and cite both.
""")
```

Three lines matter most:

**"Use only the sources above."** Without it, the model blends retrieved material with its training knowledge, and you cannot tell which is which.

**"Cite the source number."** This is what makes verification possible.

**The exact refusal wording.** Giving it a specific sentence makes refusal easy and detectable. Your code can check for that string and show a different interface.

### Formatting the sources

Number them, and include their origin:

```python
def format_sources(results: list[dict]) -> str:
    """Number the retrieved chunks so the model can cite them."""
    return "\n\n".join(
        f"[{index}] (from {result['source']}, {result.get('section', 'unknown section')})\n"
        f"{result['text']}"
        for index, result in enumerate(results, start=1)
    )
```

### The refusal path

Your application must handle two separate "I do not know" cases:

**Nothing cleared the relevance floor.** Do not call the model at all. Say the documents do not cover it. This saves a call and is more honest than letting the model decide.

**The model returned the refusal sentence.** Show it plainly, and show what was retrieved so the user can judge.

An application that always produces an answer is an application that will confidently answer questions its documents do not cover.

### Showing the sources

Always. Under every answer, show which chunks were used, with their scores, expandable to the full text.

This is not a nice extra. It is what makes the answer checkable, and it is the main advantage RAG has over asking a model directly.

## Demonstrate

The whole answer function, using the pieces from earlier lessons.

```python
from string import Template

from model import ask          # module 12
from prompts import build


RAG_SYSTEM = (
    "You answer questions strictly from provided sources. "
    "You never use outside knowledge. You always cite source numbers."
)


def answer(question: str, retrieve_fn, min_results: int = 1) -> dict:
    """Answer a question from retrieved sources.

    Returns {'answer': str, 'sources': list, 'refused': bool}.
    """
    found = retrieve_fn(question)

    # First refusal path: nothing relevant was retrieved, so do not
    # call the model at all. It would answer anyway.
    if len(found["results"]) < min_results or not found["confident"]:
        return {
            "answer": "The provided sources do not answer this question.",
            "sources": [],
            "refused": True,
        }

    prompt = build(
        RAG_PROMPT,
        sources=format_sources(found["results"]),
        question=question,
    )
    result = ask(RAG_SYSTEM, prompt)

    if not result.ok:
        return {"answer": f"Could not get an answer: {result.error}",
                "sources": found["results"], "refused": False}

    # Second refusal path: the model was given sources and still could
    # not answer from them. Show the sources so the user can judge.
    refused = "do not answer this question" in result.text.lower()

    return {"answer": result.text, "sources": found["results"], "refused": refused}
```

The two refusal paths are the substance. The first saves a pointless call; the second catches the case where retrieval found something but it did not actually help.

## Practice

Build the document question-answering application.

**Step 1.** Take a real set of documents -- your notes, a handbook, a set of papers. At least ten pages.

**Step 2.** Extract the text and **look at it**. Check for garbled columns, repeated headers, missing sections. Fix the extraction before continuing.

**Step 3.** Chunk it, with the title and section prepended to each chunk.

**Step 4.** Embed and store, with metadata including source and section.

**Step 5.** Write ten questions: **six** you know the documents answer, and **four** you know they do not.

**Step 6.** Run all ten. Score them:

- Of the six, how many were answered correctly with a correct citation?
- Of the four, how many were correctly refused?

Those two numbers are your system's quality. The second matters more, and it is the one people never measure.

:::hint It answers the four it should refuse
The most common cause is no relevance floor: retrieval always returns its top three, however irrelevant, and the model dutifully answers from them. Add the floor from lesson 4, and calibrate it by looking at what scores your four unanswerable questions actually produce. The second cause is a prompt without an explicit refusal sentence.
:::

## What to remember

- Prepend the document title and section to each chunk before embedding
- Overlap chunks so an answer straddling a boundary is not lost from both
- Tell the model to use only the sources, cite numbers, and refuse in an exact wording
- Handle two refusal paths: nothing retrieved, and retrieved but unhelpful
- Always show the sources; it is what makes the answer checkable
- Measure refusals on questions your documents cannot answer, not just correct answers

lessons.content:
Ten questions on the whole of module 13.

:::quiz
Q. What does RAG actually do?
- Trains the model on your documents
+ Finds relevant material and puts it in the prompt before asking
- Increases the model's context window
- Fine-tunes the model on retrieved examples
= The model learns nothing. It is handed the relevant passages and asked to read them, which converts recall into transformation -- module 3's safe category.

Q. Why does RAG reduce hallucination?
- The model is more careful when given sources
+ It converts recall into transformation: the material is in front of the model rather than remembered
- Retrieved text is verified before being sent
- It uses a different generation mode
= This is the central reason RAG matters. It does not eliminate hallucination -- the model can still misread a source, and a wrong source gives a confidently wrong answer with a citation attached.

Q. What is the most common cause of a bad RAG system?
- Choosing the wrong embedding model
+ Bad text extraction from the source documents
- Retrieving too few chunks
- An insufficiently capable LLM
= Garbled extraction is invisible downstream: everything looks fine and the answers are wrong. Diagnose from the start of the pipeline, not the end, because people blame the model and the fault is usually at stage one.

Q. What happens if you embed your chunks with one model and your queries with another?
- Retrieval is slightly less accurate
+ Similarity scores are meaningless, but nothing errors
- The system raises an error immediately
- Only long queries are affected
= This is an extremely confusing bug precisely because nothing fails. Store the model name with the index and refuse to search when it does not match.

Q. You have thirty pages of material that rarely changes. What should you do?
- Build a RAG pipeline with a vector database
+ Paste it into the prompt
- Fine-tune a model on it
- Chunk it and retrieve the top three per question
= If it fits in context and you want everything considered, paste it. Building RAG when pasting would do is the common and expensive mistake, and it adds a new failure mode where retrieval misses and you never find out.

Q. Roughly how many chunks before you need a vector database rather than a list and a loop?
- About a hundred
- About a thousand
+ About ten thousand
- Any amount over fifty
= Below that, a loop is exact, simple, has no extra dependency and is fast enough. The most common real trigger for a database is persistence -- not wanting to re-embed the corpus on every restart.

Q. Which single chunking change most improves retrieval quality?
- Making chunks smaller
- Increasing the overlap
+ Prepending the document title and section heading to each chunk
- Splitting at sentence boundaries
= A chunk reading "it must be returned within 14 days" is useless alone. Adding "[Employee Handbook > Section 4: Equipment]" gives it the context that makes it both retrievable and understandable, and most people do not do it.

Q. Why give the model an exact wording for refusing?
- It sounds more professional
+ It makes refusal easy for the model and detectable by your code
- It reduces token usage
- It prevents the model citing sources
= Your application can check for that specific string and show a different interface. Without a specific sentence the model produces varied hedging that you cannot reliably detect.

Q. Your system should handle two separate "I do not know" cases. What are they?
- A failed API call and an empty document set
+ Nothing cleared the relevance floor, and the model was given sources but still could not answer
- A timeout and a refusal
- An empty question and an empty corpus
= The first should skip the model call entirely, because it would answer anyway. The second means retrieval found something that did not actually help, and the sources should be shown so the user can judge.

Q. What should you measure to know whether a RAG system is any good?
- How many questions it answers
+ How many answerable questions it answers correctly, and how many unanswerable ones it correctly refuses
- Average retrieval score
- Time to first token
= The second number matters more and is the one people never measure. A system that answers everything is a system that confidently answers questions its documents do not cover.
:::

## How to read your score

Seven or more and you are ready for the capstone. If you missed questions, the most useful correction is to build the small pipeline from lesson 2 and deliberately make it fail -- this module's ideas land once you have watched retrieval miss.

lessons.title: Hands-on lab: RAG over your own notes
lessons.description: Build it over your own material, then measure the number nobody measures.
lessons.content:
Sixty minutes. You will build RAG over your own notes, then measure how good it actually is.

The measurement is the point. Anyone can build something that answers questions; knowing whether it answers them correctly is the skill.

## Before you start

```bash
pip install sentence-transformers numpy
```

Gather **your own** material: lecture notes, a handbook, documentation, a set of papers. At least ten pages of real text. Your own material matters -- you can tell whether the answers are right.

## Step 1: Extract and look at it

Get the text into a file or a list of strings.

Then **read it**. Genuinely read a page of it.

Check for: garbled columns from PDF extraction, headers and footers repeating, missing sections, run-together words, tables turned into nonsense.

Fix what you find before continuing. This step is skipped by almost everyone and causes most of the problems later.

Record what you had to fix.

## Step 2: Chunk it

Write a chunker that splits at paragraph boundaries, keeps chunks under a size limit, overlaps slightly, and **prepends the document title and section heading**.

Then inspect the output: print five random chunks and read them.

Ask of each: could someone understand this on its own? If not, your chunks lack context and the fix is in step 2, not later.

## Step 3: Embed and store

Embed all chunks. Save vectors and metadata to disk, keeping them in the same order.

Store for each chunk: the text, the source file, the section, and its position.

Record how long embedding took and how many chunks you have.

## Step 4: Retrieve

Write `search(question, top_k, min_score)` returning results with scores and metadata, and a `confident` flag.

Test it with three questions and look at the scores. Note the range -- you will need it to set the floor.

## Step 5: The test set

The most important step. Write **fifteen** questions:

- **Ten** you know your documents answer. For each, write down the correct answer and which section it is in.
- **Five** you know your documents do **not** answer. Plausible questions about the same subject area, not nonsense.

Write these **before** running anything, so you are not testing what the system happens to do well.

## Step 6: Measure retrieval alone

Before involving a model, check whether retrieval works.

For each of the ten answerable questions, run `search` and record: was the correct chunk in the top three?

That number is your **retrieval accuracy**. If it is below about seven in ten, fix retrieval before going further -- no prompt can compensate for the right passage not being found.

:::hint My retrieval accuracy is poor
Check in this order. First, are your chunks understandable alone? If not, go back to step 2 and add the title and section prefix. Second, are chunks too large, so the relevant sentence is diluted by surrounding text? Third, is the answer split across two chunks, which more overlap would fix? Fourth, and only then, consider a different embedding model. The fault is almost never the model.
:::

## Step 7: Generate

Add the prompt and answer function from lesson 5, with both refusal paths.

If you have no API access, do this step by hand: print the assembled prompt, paste it into any chat tool, and record the answer. The measurement works the same way.

## Step 8: Measure the whole system

Run all fifteen questions.

**For the ten answerable:**
- Correct answer? Yes or no.
- Correct citation? Yes or no.

**For the five unanswerable:**
- Correctly refused? Yes or no.

Three numbers: answer accuracy, citation accuracy, refusal rate.

The refusal rate is the one that matters most and the one nobody measures.

## Step 9: Improve one thing

Find your weakest number. Change **one** thing:

- Poor retrieval: chunk size, overlap, or the section prefix
- Poor refusal: add or raise the relevance floor, or strengthen the refusal instruction
- Poor citation: strengthen the citation instruction

Re-run all fifteen. Record the before and after.

## Step 10: Write it up

1. Your material, and what you fixed in extraction
2. Chunking: size, overlap, prefix, and how many chunks
3. Retrieval accuracy on the ten
4. The three system numbers
5. The one change you made, and the before and after
6. One question it got wrong, with your diagnosis of which pipeline stage caused it

## What good looks like

A strong submission has **all three numbers, before and after a change**, and a diagnosis in step 10 that names a pipeline stage rather than blaming the model.

The single most valuable thing you can report is a low refusal rate that you then fixed. A system that answers all five unanswerable questions is the normal first result, and noticing it is the finding.

lessons.title: Assignment: a document assistant with citations
lessons.description: A working system plus an honest evaluation, marked against a rubric.
lessons.content:
## The task

Build a document assistant with citations over a real document set, and evaluate it honestly.

The evaluation is the substance. A RAG system nobody measured is a RAG system nobody knows the quality of.

## Choose a real document set

Something you know well enough to mark answers against. Your course notes, a workplace handbook, a set of papers, documentation for a tool you use, the rules of a society.

**At least twenty pages.** It must be material where you can tell whether an answer is right.

If the material is confidential, check module 10 first: if it cannot go into a tool, either use different material or run an embedding model locally, which `sentence-transformers` does by default.

## What to submit

The **code**, and a document of **1000 to 1400 words**.

### The application

- Ingests your documents, chunks, embeds and stores them
- Answers questions from retrieved sources
- **Shows the sources used for every answer**, with scores
- **Refuses** when the sources do not cover the question
- Handles empty input and a failed model call
- Runs from a clean checkout with a README

No hard-coded keys. `.env.example` present, `.env` absent.

An interface is welcome but not required. A command-line tool is fine.

### The document

**1. The document set.** What it is, how much, what extraction problems you hit and how you fixed them.

**2. Chunking decisions.** Size, overlap, boundaries, what you prepend. Why those choices, and what you tried that was worse.

**3. Retrieval.** Embedding model, store, top-k, relevance floor and how you calibrated it.

**4. The prompt.** In full, with a note on each rule and what happens without it. For at least one rule, show evidence: what the output looked like before and after.

**5. The evaluation.** The heaviest-marked section.

- Your test set: **minimum 20 questions**, at least **6 unanswerable**
- Retrieval accuracy: was the right chunk in the top k?
- Answer accuracy on the answerable questions
- Citation accuracy: did the citation point at the passage the answer came from?
- **Refusal rate** on the unanswerable questions
- The full results, not just totals

**6. Failure analysis.** Take **three** questions it got wrong. For each, diagnose which pipeline stage caused it -- extraction, chunking, embedding, retrieval or generation -- with the evidence for that diagnosis.

**7. One improvement.** One change, with before and after numbers.

**8. Honest limits.** What this system is not good at, and what you would not use it for.

## Rubric

Marked out of 100.

**The application works, 20 marks.** Full marks for a system that ingests, retrieves, answers, cites and refuses, running from a clean checkout. Marks lost for any missing capability, and heavily for a system that cannot refuse.

**Pipeline decisions, 15 marks.** Full marks for chunking and retrieval choices that are explained and justified, including what you tried that was worse. Marks lost for defaults adopted without comment.

**The prompt, 10 marks.** Full marks for a prompt with source-only, citation and exact-refusal rules, with evidence for at least one.

**Evaluation, 30 marks.** Full marks for at least 20 questions including at least 6 unanswerable, all four measurements, and the full results shown. The heaviest section. **An evaluation without unanswerable questions cannot score above half**, because the refusal rate is the number that matters most.

**Failure analysis, 15 marks.** Full marks for three failures each diagnosed to a specific pipeline stage with evidence. Marks lost for "the model got it wrong", which names no stage.

**Improvement and limits, 10 marks.** Full marks for one change with before-and-after numbers, plus a specific account of what the system is not good at.

## What will cost you marks

**No unanswerable questions in the test set.** This is the most common failure and it costs heavily. A system that answers everything looks perfect until you ask it something the documents do not cover.

**Blaming the model.** Every failure has a stage. Extraction, chunking, embedding, retrieval or generation. Name it and show why.

**Totals without the underlying results.** Show the per-question table.

**An improvement with no numbers.** "It seemed better afterwards" is not evidence.

**A key in the repository.** Check the history.

:::hint My refusal rate is zero and I cannot fix it
That is the normal first result, and fixing it is worth real marks. Three causes, in order of likelihood. One: no relevance floor, so retrieval always returns its top three however irrelevant, and the model answers from them -- add the floor and calibrate it against the scores your unanswerable questions actually produce. Two: no exact refusal wording in the prompt, so the model hedges rather than refusing and you cannot detect it. Three: your unanswerable questions are too close to your material -- if you asked about a topic the documents mention in passing, the system is arguably right to attempt an answer, and you should sharpen the question instead.
:::

lessons.title: Level 2 exam: GenAI Practitioner
lessons.description: Twenty questions and two applied tasks covering modules 6 to 13.
lessons.content:
This is the **Level 2 certification exam: GenAI Practitioner**. It covers modules 6 to 13.

## Before you start

**One sitting, no notes, no AI tool open.**

Twenty questions, then two applied tasks. Expect about fifty minutes.

This exam is more applied than Level 1. Several questions describe a situation and ask what you would do, and the marks are for judgement rather than recall.

**Pass mark: 14 out of 20 on the questions.**

:::quiz
Q. Which research request is safe, and which is not?
- Both "summarise this paper I uploaded" and "list five papers on this topic" are safe
+ Uploading a paper and asking about it is safe; asking for a list of papers is not
- Both are unsafe without a search tool
- It depends on how recent the topic is
= The first is transformation of material in front of the model. The second is recall of facts, which is where invention clusters. Use databases to find and AI to understand what you found.

Q. You ask a model to total a column of twenty figures. What should you do instead?
- Ask it to check its own arithmetic
- Ask twice and compare
+ Ask for the formula and let the spreadsheet compute
- Break the column into smaller groups
= A language model produces plausible-looking numbers rather than calculated ones. Formulas yes, figures no -- and the same applies to reading values off a screenshot.

Q. A generated image of "a person holding up five fingers next to a shop sign" comes out wrong. Which explanation fits?
- The prompt was too short
+ Hands and readable text need exact structure, which a statistical process does not enforce
- Image models cannot render people
- The resolution was too low
= Style transfers reliably because it is a broad statistical property. Fingers, letterforms and exact counts need precision the statistics do not guarantee.

Q. Which addition typically changes a generated image most?
- "high quality, 8k, masterpiece"
+ A style word such as "watercolour" or "film photograph"
- More adjectives about the subject
- A longer, more detailed prompt
= Style is the highest-leverage word in any image prompt. Adjectives of approval do almost nothing; the model has no reliable notion of "masterpiece" separate from what it does anyway.

Q. You need a specific arrangement in an image -- this object left, that one behind. What works best?
- A more precise text description
- Repeating the spatial instruction
+ Sketching the layout and using image-to-image
- A negative prompt for the wrong arrangement
= Text prompts control arrangement poorly because you are nudging a process rather than commanding it. A sketch supplies composition directly and the text controls appearance.

Q. What is the rule for putting text on a generated poster?
- Generate it with the text, then fix errors by inpainting
+ Generate the artwork with no text, then add text in a design tool
- Use a model that specialises in typography
- Generate text and image separately and combine them with a third prompt
= Text inside generated images is unreliable, and even when legible you cannot control font, spacing and alignment -- which is what a poster depends on.

Q. Someone asks you to clone a colleague's voice for an internal joke video. What is the correct response?
- Do it, but disclose it in the video
- Do it only if the video stays internal
+ Refuse; a voice may not be cloned without that person's explicit, informed consent
- Do it using a stock voice that sounds similar
= No exception for jokes, internal use or public figures. Cloning needs very little source audio and is the basis of a common and effective fraud.

Q. Which AI capability has changed video production most in practice?
- Text-to-video generation
- AI avatars
+ Transcript-based editing, captions and audio cleanup
- AI music generation
= Generation still produces material that mostly does not work. Editing tools do genuinely tedious jobs reliably on real footage, and a two-hour edit becoming twenty minutes is the larger change.

Q. A generated function uses `list.sort` on the list it was given. Why does that matter?
- `sort` is slower than `sorted`
+ It modifies the caller's list as a side effect, causing bugs elsewhere that are hard to trace
- `sort` cannot take a key function
- It fails on empty input
= Generated code often uses in-place operations where a copy was wanted, because in isolation it looks correct. The damage appears in a different function later and looks like a bug there.

Q. Which is the more expensive kind of bug, and why?
- A loud one, because it stops the program
+ A quiet one, because it produces plausible wrong output with nothing to signal it
- A loud one, because the traceback can be misleading
- They cost about the same
= A loud bug names its own line. A quiet one returns wrong answers indefinitely, which is why you run generated code rather than reading it approvingly.

Q. You are given generated comments that restate what each line does. What should you have asked for?
- Shorter comments
+ Comments explaining why each non-obvious decision was made, with a TODO where it cannot tell
- Docstrings instead of comments
- Comments only on the complex lines
= The code already says what. Only a person knows why. Without the TODO clause the model invents a rationale, which is worse than no comment because it will be believed.

Q. A hundred apparently independent sources agree on a claim. Why is that weaker evidence than it used to be?
- Sources copy each other more than they did
+ Producing a hundred plausible variants now costs almost nothing, so apparent independence can be manufactured
- Search engines rank duplicates higher
- Fact-checking has not kept pace
= The falsehoods are not new; the economics collapsed. This defeats corroboration, which is the heuristic most people rely on, and the defence is tracing to the primary source.

Q. Why does prompt injection have no complete fix?
- Providers have not prioritised it
+ A model cannot reliably distinguish your instructions from text inside the content you gave it
- It only affects tools with internet access
- It requires knowing the system prompt
= Mitigations reduce it; none removes it. Design assuming it can happen, limit what any tool can reach, and keep a human confirming anything irreversible.

Q. Your team wants AI to shortlist job applicants. What is the correct position?
- Use it, with a human reviewing the shortlist
- Use it only for an initial filter on qualifications
+ Do not use it; the bias becomes a decision about people, at scale and invisibly
- Use it if the model is audited for bias
= The firmest rule in the ethics module. You will not be able to show the bias did not affect the outcome, and the harm falls on people who cannot see it happening.

Q. What distinguishes an agent from a workflow?
- The agent uses a more capable model
+ In a workflow you decide the sequence; in an agent the model does
- The agent has memory between sessions
- The agent can call external APIs
= The difference is who decides the sequence, and it sets your blast radius. If you can write the steps down, write them down -- you get predictability for free.

Q. Ten agent steps each succeeding ninety per cent of the time gives roughly what end-to-end reliability?
- About ninety per cent
- About eighty per cent
+ About thirty-five per cent
- About ten per cent
= Errors compound multiplicatively. This is the central practical problem with agents and the reason to keep tasks small.

Q. When a model requests a tool call, what actually happens?
- The model runs the function in a sandbox
+ It produces a structured request, and your code decides whether to run it
- The platform executes it automatically
- The function runs with the model's own permissions
= The model never executes anything. All your control -- confirmation, validation, permission limits, logging -- lives in the gap between the request and the action.

Q. Your agent tool hits an error. What should it return?
- Raise the exception so the loop stops
+ A readable error message the model can act on
- Nothing, and retry silently
- The full stack trace
= An agent that receives a readable error can try something else. One that crashes the program cannot. "No customer found with that email" is useful; a traceback ends the run.

Q. You have thirty pages of material that rarely changes. What should you build?
- A RAG pipeline with a vector database
+ Nothing -- paste it into the prompt
- A fine-tuned model
- An agent that retrieves sections on demand
= If it fits in context and you want everything considered, paste it. Building RAG when pasting would do adds a new failure mode where retrieval misses and you never find out.

Q. Your RAG system answers every question, including ones your documents do not cover. What is the most likely cause?
- The embedding model is too weak
- The chunks are too large
+ There is no relevance floor, so retrieval always returns its top results and the model answers from them
- The prompt is too short
= Retrieval always returns something. Without a floor, irrelevant chunks are passed to a model that will dutifully answer from them. A specific refusal wording in the prompt is the second half of the fix.
:::

## The applied section

Both tasks. Together they carry as much weight as the questions.

### Task 1: diagnose a RAG failure

A colleague's document assistant answers well on most questions but has these three problems:

1. It answers questions the documents do not cover, confidently
2. One answer was correct but cited the wrong page
3. Questions about a policy in the appendix always fail, though the appendix is in the source PDF

For **each**, name the pipeline stage responsible -- extraction, chunking, embedding, retrieval or generation -- say what evidence would confirm your diagnosis, and state the fix.

### Task 2: design the safety layer

You are asked to build an agent that reads incoming supplier emails, looks up the supplier in a database, and drafts a reply.

State:

1. The tools it needs, and for each whether it is read-only
2. Which actions require human confirmation, and why those
3. Your step limit, and how you chose the number
4. One prompt-injection scenario specific to this agent, and what contains it

## Marking

**The questions: 20 marks**, one each. Pass is 14.

**Task 1: 12 marks**, four per problem. Full marks require naming the stage, the confirming evidence and the fix. Expected: (1) retrieval or generation -- no relevance floor and no refusal instruction; (2) generation or chunking -- the citation metadata is misaligned with the chunk, check that vectors and metadata are in the same order; (3) extraction -- the appendix is likely a scanned page yielding no text, check the extracted output directly.

**Task 2: 8 marks.** Two per part. Full marks for a read-only lookup tool separated from any sending tool, confirmation on anything that leaves the organisation, a stated step limit with a reason, and an injection scenario naming the email body as the untrusted content.

**Total: 40 marks. Pass: 28.**

## If you do not pass

The applied tasks are where most people lose marks, and they are the better guide to what to revisit. Naming a pipeline stage rather than blaming the model, and knowing where a human belongs in an agent loop, are the two judgements this level certifies.
